messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Jeweler
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 54

**Vignette: Margaret, Age 50**

Margaret has spent most of her adult life working with her hands. For nearly two decades, she has run a small jewelry studio out of a rented storefront in a mid-sized city, crafting custom pieces for clients who come to her by word of mouth. She is precise, patient, and takes pride in the intimacy of her work — the way a ring or a pendant can carry someone's most important memories. Until about fourteen months ago, she says, her life felt quiet in a way she had earned.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Margaret was locking up the studio after a long day when a man she did not recognize pushed her back through the door. He demanded the contents of the display case. When she hesitated, he struck her twice across the face and shoved her to the floor, stepping on her right hand before grabbing what he could and running. She lay on the cold tile for several minutes before she was able to call for help. Her hand — the hand she uses to set stones, to solder, to do the most delicate work of her life — sustained a fracture that required surgery and months of rehabilitation.

The physical healing has largely progressed, though she still notices stiffness in cold weather. What has not healed follows a different anatomy altogether.

In the weeks after the assault, Margaret found she could not sleep for more than two or three hours at a stretch. She would wake with her heart pounding, certain she could hear someone in the studio below her apartment, and lie rigid in the dark until dawn made the fear manageable. She returned to work after six weeks because she had no choice financially, but standing behind the display case — the same case he had emptied — produced a tightening in her chest she could not reason away. She rearranged the studio twice, moved the case, changed the lighting, and still the feeling came.

Now, more than a year later, the hypervigilance has become the texture of her daily life. She scans every customer who walks through the door. Men who move too quickly or stand too close cause her breath to go shallow. She has installed two additional locks and a security camera, and she checks the footage each morning before opening. She knows, intellectually, that these measures are reasonable. She also knows that reasonable measures are not what drives her to check the locks four and five times before she can sleep.

The intrusions arrive without warning. She can be in the middle of soldering a setting, fully absorbed, and suddenly she is back on the tile floor, looking up at the ceiling of her own studio, feeling the weight of a boot on her hand. She puts down her tools and waits for it to pass. Sometimes it takes minutes. Sometimes she closes early.

What troubles her most, she says, is what the assault has done to the meaning of her work. Jewelry used to feel like an act of care — she was making something that would outlast her, something that would be handed down. Now, when she handles a piece, she is sometimes aware only of how fragile everything is, how quickly a life can be interrupted. She has turned down two large commissions in the past six months, telling clients she is backed up, when the truth is she cannot sustain the concentration the work requires.

Margaret describes herself as someone who has always handled things on her own. She is single, lives alone, and has a small circle of friends she has gradually been seeing less of, partly because she does not want to talk about what happened and partly because the effort of performing normalcy exhausts her. She came to therapy, she says, not because she thinks talking will fix anything, but because she has started to feel like a stranger in the studio that used to be the place she felt most like herself.
